To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the electrically evokes compound action potentials in the human cochlea can be simulated with a two-component model, that this model can be used to explain the various NRT waveforms, and that the two-component model may be used to determine the optimal speech coding parameters in cochlear implants.

The electrically evoked NRT waveforms in the human cochlea can be simulated by linearly combining two separate waveforms, one with a shorter and the other with a longer latency, similar in shape but with differing amplitudes.

1) the electrically evoking compound action potential in the human cochlea is a composite of at least two components, 2) these components are likely to originate from dendritic and axonal processes and 3) the shape of the NRT waveform may provide information on the degree of neural survivability in the stimulated cochlear.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the neural response to electric stimulation in the human cochlea and the development of a mathematical model that could be used to simulate the electrically evoking compound action potential (ECAP) recorded from the auditory nerve.
the development and application of a mathematical model of the electrically stimulated auditory nerve in order to gain a better understanding of cochlear implant performance.
the development of an accurate and efficient model to predict the electrically evoking compound action potential in the human cochlea.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the double peak waveform originates from two components, the first originating from dendritic and the second originating from axonal processes.
the two components are not dendritic and axonal but are instead the result of the interaction between the electric field and the neural processes.
the double positive peak NRT waveform is not a reliable predictor of the degree of neural preservation and/or the degree of residual hearing.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a simple model of NRT waveforms is possible and that this model could provide information regarding the neural survival and function in cochleas of cochlear implant users.
the NRT response waveform is a good indicator of the state of the neural survival in the cochlea.
NRT waveforms may contain valuable information about the state of the neural elements of the cochlea and that such information may be useful for the optimization of cochlear implant performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NRT recordings can be used for estimating the relative contributions of the axonal and dendritically driven components of the compound action potential in the human cochlea.
the NRT waveforms may contain useful information about the degree to which the cochlea is stimulated by the electrode array.

a simple two-component model of the electrically-evoked compound action potential in the human cochlea can explain the various waveform categories that are commonly observed in neural response telemetry (NRTL) recordings.
